prompt: Why isn't a GitHub profile README (the special username/username repo) a substitute for a deployed portfolio site?
choices: It can't contain any Markdown formatting at all
It only renders inside GitHub's own page chrome, so you don't control layout and it's one extra click away from non-GitHub users like a hiring manager
GitHub profile READMEs are deprecated and no longer render on profile pages
It requires a paid GitHub account to display

prompt: On a portfolio project card, what should the 'Architecture' section of Tier 1's four-part README structure compress down to?
choices: A full prose paragraph explaining data flow between modules, same length as in the README
Nothing - architecture should be omitted entirely from a card
A short row of stack tags that signal real tools at a glance, without explaining data flow
A link to the project's full commit history

prompt: You push a portfolio site to a GitHub repo named 'my-portfolio' (not 'yourusername.github.io') and want GitHub Pages to serve it from the main branch. What's the correct step?
choices: Nothing - GitHub Pages serves any repo automatically regardless of its name
Rename the repo to exactly match your GitHub username with no other option
In that repo's Settings > Pages, set Source to 'Deploy from a branch', pick main and /(root) - it then serves at https://yourusername.github.io/my-portfolio/
Install a separate GitHub Pages app from the marketplace before any repo can use Pages

prompt: TrailLink's 'Live demo' link needs to point at a real running Flask API, not a static file. Per this lesson, what's the correct way to get that live URL?
choices: Re-derive container deployment from scratch, since portfolio deployment and API deployment are unrelated problems
Reuse the Dockerfile + fly launch --no-deploy + fly deploy flow already taught in Platforms Tier 3's Cloud Basics for App Backends module, pointed at the actual TrailLink app
Upload the Flask app's source files directly to GitHub Pages alongside the static HTML
Embed the Flask app's Python code directly inside the portfolio's index.html

prompt: A specialization project like portwatch.py is a lab-only security tool with nothing safe to deploy publicly. What does this lesson say the portfolio card for it should do?
choices: Fake a live demo link anyway so the card looks complete
Skip the project entirely and only show cards for projects with live demos
Include only a source link and omit the 'Live demo' link - an honest omission, not a gap, since a fake live link that 404s is worse
Deploy the tool publicly regardless of the security risk, just to have a live link

prompt: Why does this lesson say the open-source contributions list (merged PRs) is arguably the highest-signal section on the whole portfolio page?
choices: It's the easiest section to build, requiring no HTML at all
It proves a stranger with no relationship to the learner decided their code was good enough to merge into something they maintain - a kind of proof no side project carries
It's required by GitHub Pages for the site to be indexed by search engines
It replaces the need for any project cards on the page

prompt: What is the correct way to compress a project's full four-part README Problem+Solution into 2-3 sentences for a portfolio card, per this lesson's hint?
choices: Write the short card version from scratch without reference to the full README
Write or reuse the full four-part README first, then delete sentences from Problem+Solution one at a time until only what a stranger needs to decide 'worth clicking into' remains
Copy the README's License section since it's already short
Use an AI tool to summarize the entire README into one word
